units.title: Unit 51 — Starting and finishing
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 106–107 (PDF pages 110–111).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Use natural expressions to describe promising, early and disappointing beginnings.
Describe close or tense finishes and distinguish finishing touches from the end result.
Contrast get started, make a start, come to an end, draw to a close and bring something to an end.
Avoid the learner error of using finish instead of end for holidays and journeys.

items.example: The new research partnership could make a promising start with this pilot study.
items.note: Use make with start when describing an encouraging beginning; a promising start suggests potential, not certain success.

items.example: We should make an early start to avoid the busiest roads.
items.note: An early start means beginning an activity or journey earlier than usual; use make, not do.

items.pt: iniciante absoluto; pessoa sem conhecimentos prévios
items.example: The course is suitable for an absolute beginner who has never studied German.
items.note: Absolute intensifies beginner to indicate no previous knowledge or experience.

items.word: get off to a good start
items.pt: começar bem; ter um bom começo
items.example: Our presentation got off to a good start with a clear introduction.
items.note: Get off to a good start is an idiomatic way to describe the initial stage of an activity, event or relationship.

items.pt: disputa acirrada na chegada; final apertado
items.example: The cycling race ended in a close finish between two teammates.
items.note: A close finish is an outcome in which competitors are separated by very little, especially in sport.

items.pt: final emocionante; desfecho de tirar o fôlego
items.example: The final set gave spectators a nail-biting finish to the tennis match.
items.note: Nail-biting describes excitement and tension when the outcome is uncertain until the end.

items.word: put the finishing touches to a report
items.pt: dar os retoques finais em um relatório
items.example: We need to put the finishing touches to a report before sending it.
items.note: British English often uses put the finishing touches to; put the finishing touches on is also common.

items.word: bring a strike to an end
items.example: A signed agreement can bring a strike to an end.
items.note: Bring something to an end means cause it to stop; unlike come to an end, it names an active cause.

items.word: mark the beginning of the end
items.section: C · More ways to start and finish
items.example: Losing its main sponsor could mark the beginning of the end for the team.
items.note: This expression signals the first sign that something is likely to decline or cease.

items.section: C · More ways to start and finish
items.example: The end result of the redesign was a lighter and more reliable device.
items.note: End result refers to the final outcome, not the act of finishing.

items.word: a perfect end to a holiday
items.pt: um encerramento perfeito para as férias
items.section: C · More ways to start and finish
items.example: A quiet evening by the sea was a perfect end to a holiday.
items.note: The noun end commonly takes to when it means the conclusion of an experience.

items.section: C · More ways to start and finish
items.example: Everyone is ready, so we can make a start on the installation.
items.note: Make a start means begin, often after preparation or a delay; do a start is unnatural.

items.section: C · More ways to start and finish
items.example: We can get started as soon as the equipment is ready.
items.note: Get started is a conversational way of inviting or telling people to begin.

items.section: C · More ways to start and finish
items.example: The training programme will come to an end next Friday.
items.note: Come to an end is intransitive: it describes the event ending without naming the person who ends it.

items.pt: aproximar-se do fim; chegar ao encerramento
items.section: C · More ways to start and finish
items.example: As the discussion began to draw to a close, we agreed on the next steps.
items.note: A moderately formal alternative to come to an end, especially for meetings, periods or events.

items.section: C · More ways to start and finish
items.example: The funding cut brought the project to an abrupt end.
items.note: Abrupt suggests something ends suddenly, often unexpectedly or without preparation.

items.pt: um começo tardio; início mais tarde
items.example: After a late start, the walkers reached the campsite at sunset.
items.note: Contrasts with an early start; make a late start is also possible.

items.word: get off to a disappointing start
items.pt: começar de maneira decepcionante; começar mal
items.example: The launch got off to a disappointing start because of repeated technical problems.
items.note: Get off to describes how something begins; a good, promising or disappointing start is possible.

items.word: bring a career to an abrupt end
items.example: An unexpected injury can bring a career to an abrupt end.
items.note: This is the causative counterpart of come to an end. A noun such as career, discussion or event normally replaces something.

items.example: My neighbour joined an absolute beginners’ class in Italian.
items.note: The plural possessive beginners’ identifies a class intended for people with no prior experience.

items.example: Our journey ended at a small station near the coast.
items.note: For a journey, trip, holiday or meal, ended is normally more idiomatic than finished.

sectionsChecked: A · Starting: news-style collocations and absolute beginners
B · Finishing: close/nail-biting outcomes, final touches and ending a strike

units.title: Unit 52 — Talking about success and failure
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 108–109 (PDF pages 112–113).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Discuss achievement, improvement, progress and effective contributions with natural collocations.
Distinguish breakthrough, crowning achievement, a great success and successful performance.
Describe degrees and types of failure, including flop, dismal failure and doomed to failure.
Use figurative expressions such as dash hopes, lose your nerve and miss the point appropriately.

items.pt: conseguir um avanço importante; alcançar uma descoberta significativa
items.example: The engineers hope to make a breakthrough in battery performance.
items.note: A breakthrough is an important advance after difficulty or sustained effort; make is the standard verb.

items.pt: uma conquista notável; um feito extraordinário
items.example: Completing the project in six weeks was a remarkable achievement.
items.note: Remarkable emphasises how unusual or impressive an accomplishment is.

items.pt: uma melhora expressiva; uma melhoria marcante
items.example: There has been a dramatic improvement in the software’s response time.
items.note: Dramatic here means very large and noticeable, not theatrical.

items.example: Winning the research prize was the crowning achievement of her career.
items.note: A crowning achievement is someone’s greatest or most satisfying success, often after many other achievements.

items.pt: um excelente domínio do inglês; ótima compreensão do inglês
items.example: She has an excellent grasp of the fundamentals of electronics.
items.note: Grasp here means understanding or command of a subject, not physical holding.

items.example: Your programming experience may come in useful during the internship.
items.note: Informal but standard British English expression: a skill or object proves useful when needed.

items.example: Students should take advantage of an opportunity to practise speaking.
items.note: Usually means make good use of an opportunity; it can also mean exploit someone unfairly in other contexts.

items.pt: passar em uma prova; ser aprovado em um exame
items.example: You must pass an exam before receiving the certificate.
items.note: Pass an exam contrasts with fail an exam; do an exam means sit or take the test, not necessarily succeed.

items.example: Careful planning helps, but it does not mean guaranteed success.
items.note: Guaranteed describes an outcome presented as certain; avoid using it for merely likely success.

items.example: The trainee continues to make good progress in technical English.
items.note: Progress is normally uncountable in this meaning; make progress, not do progress.

items.pt: tirar boas notas; obter boas notas
items.example: He worked hard all term to gain good marks in physics.
items.note: British English uses marks for grades or scores in school; get good marks is also common.

items.example: The community science event was a great success.
items.note: A success refers to something that succeeds; success alone is usually uncountable when used generally.

items.example: The new training method proved highly effective for beginners.
items.note: Highly, rather than very highly or strongly, is a natural intensifier with effective.

items.pt: dar contribuições úteis; contribuir de forma relevante
items.example: Several volunteers make useful contributions to the discussion each week.
items.note: Make a contribution is standard; useful describes an input that helps a discussion, project or community.

items.example: Many people have the ability to learn complex skills with practice.
items.note: Ability is commonly followed by to plus an infinitive; compare have the skills to.

items.example: The team explored effective ways of working across different time zones.
items.note: Effective ways of working describes methods that achieve the intended result.

items.example: The pilot programme was a brilliant success despite its limited budget.
items.note: Brilliant is enthusiastic and somewhat informal, stronger than a basic positive assessment.

items.word: enjoy the fruits of hard work
items.pt: colher os frutos do trabalho árduo
items.example: After years of training, she can finally enjoy the fruits of hard work.
items.note: Fruits is figurative: the benefits or rewards produced by effort.

items.word: bring out the best in people
items.example: A supportive manager can bring out the best in people.
items.note: The phrase describes helping someone show their strongest qualities or performance.

items.example: You can win the respect of others by keeping your promises.
items.note: Win respect means earn it through actions; respect is not literally awarded as a prize.

items.pt: fracassar completamente; falhar de maneira desastrosa
items.example: The advertising campaign could fail miserably if the message is unclear.
items.note: Miserably is a strong intensifier meaning very badly; it does not imply sadness in this use.

items.example: The expensive prototype turned out to be a spectacular failure.
items.note: Spectacular modifies failure to emphasise an especially striking or public lack of success.

items.example: The play flopped despite positive reviews.
items.note: Flop is informal and commonly describes unsuccessful shows, films, books or products.

items.pt: as esperanças foram destruídas; as expectativas foram frustradas
items.example: Their hopes were dashed when the grant application was rejected.
items.note: Dash someone’s hopes means suddenly destroy expectations or plans; a fixed passive pattern is common.

items.example: If you fail your final exams, the school may offer another chance.
items.note: Fail takes an exam as its object; this contrasts with pass your exams.

items.example: The expedition could go badly wrong without suitable equipment.
items.note: Go wrong means develop problems; badly intensifies the extent of the failure.

items.example: Without a clear plan, the negotiation may be doomed to failure.
items.note: A strong prediction that an effort is virtually certain not to succeed.

items.example: The first attempt was a dismal failure, but the second worked well.
items.note: Dismal conveys very poor results and disappointment; dismal fail is ungrammatical here.

items.pt: fechar as portas; encerrar as atividades comerciais
items.example: Small shops may go out of business when costs rise too quickly.
items.note: Used when a company or shop stops trading, particularly for financial reasons.

items.pt: receita para o desastre; situação com grande risco de dar errado
items.example: Skipping safety checks is a recipe for disaster in a laboratory.
items.note: A figurative expression for a plan or combination of conditions very likely to cause serious problems.

items.example: Do not lose your nerve just before the interview.
items.note: Lose your nerve means suddenly become too frightened or hesitant to do what you intended.

items.pt: não entender o ponto principal; não captar a ideia
items.example: You miss the point if you focus only on the price and ignore reliability.
items.note: Means misunderstand the central idea; miss the point is different from make a point.

items.pt: dar uma contribuição enorme; contribuir imensamente
items.example: Her mentor continues to make an enormous contribution to local education.
items.note: Use make with contribution; enormous strongly emphasises its extent.

items.example: The first version of the app was a complete flop with users.
items.note: Flop is a noun for an unsuccessful effort or product; an informal alternative to failure.

items.example: We had high hopes for the new scheme, but the results were disappointing.
items.note: High naturally combines with hopes; the phrase expresses optimistic expectations.

items.pt: alguém excepcional no aprendizado de idiomas
items.example: Everyone expected him to be a brilliant language learner after his first course.
items.note: Brilliant is a strong, positive adjective for ability or performance; this item is from the exercise context.

items.pt: ir mal na escola; fracassar nos estudos
items.example: Children who fail at school may succeed in practical training.
items.note: Fail at school means perform poorly overall, whereas fail an exam identifies a particular test.
